title: How Centene Is Bringing Maternal Care Closer to Rural Communities
summary: See how Centene combines care coordination, virtual maternity expertise and local providers to expand access maternal health care in rural communities.
body_markdown:
For individuals who are pregnant and live in rural communities, getting maternity care can mean traveling farther, navigating provider shortages or having limited access to specialists. According to the[March of Dimes,](https://www.marchofdimes.org/peristats/assets/s3/reports/2026-Maternity-Care-Report.pdf) one in three U.S. counties is considered a maternity care desert, meaning it has no hospital or birth center offering obstetric care and no obstetric clinicians. Nearly 70% of maternity care deserts are rural.


These challenges can extend beyond obstetric care. Rural communities may also have limited access to behavioral health services, transportation and other resources that support a healthy pregnancy and postpartum recovery.


For Centene,[addressing those gaps](https://www.centene.com/why-were-different/improving-outcomes/maternal-and-child-health.html) is particularly important because of the scale and diversity of the communities its health plans serve. Centene manages more than 290,000 deliveries annually*, approximately 90% through Medicaid. Across the 2,420 counties in 33 states that Centene serves, more than 48% have limited or no maternity care access, including 839 maternity care deserts.


That reach creates an opportunity to identify where care gaps exist and connect members with the right support, including bringing additional expertise into communities where it may not otherwise be readily available.


## Connecting Members to the Right Maternal Care


Pregnancy and postpartum care rarely happen in a single setting. Members may need obstetric care, specialty care, behavioral health services, transportation or community-based support at different points throughout their care journey.


Managed care can help connect those pieces. Centene health plans use population, claims, authorization and risk information to better understand members’ needs and identify potential barriers to care. Care coordination, including outreach and care management, can then help members connect with available providers, covered benefits and community resources that meet their needs.


This approach also helps health plans understand where broader access gaps exist and identify different ways to address them. In some communities, that may mean working with local providers and organizations. In others, virtual care can add clinical capacity and make specialized expertise available without requiring every service to be located nearby.


## How Virtual Maternity Care Adds Expertise in Rural Communities


Virtual care is a critical tool Centene uses to help connect members with needed services. A pilot partnership with[Ouma Health](https://www.oumahealth.com/) and Centene health plans, beginning with Sunshine Health in Florida, offers a maternity-focused example of how that approach can help extend clinical expertise into communities with limited access.


Ouma provides virtual maternity services that can either supplement local care or provide more comprehensive support when certain services are difficult to access. Its clinical team includes maternity specialists who can provide prenatal and postpartum care, maternal-fetal medicine (MFM) consultations, behavioral health and substance use care, and lactation support. Ouma also provides remote monitoring that helps clinicians stay connected with patients between visits.


The goal is not simply to replace an in-person visit with a virtual one. It is to give members another way to reach maternity expertise when distance, provider shortages or other barriers make that expertise difficult to access locally.


## Connecting Virtual and Local Care


Effective virtual maternity care requires coordination across the member’s care team.


Centene health plans can use information about their populations to identify needs, engage members and help coordinate covered benefits and community resources. Ouma adds virtual maternity expertise, monitoring, navigation and clinical escalation. When local providers are available, they continue providing in-person care and maintaining established relationships with patients in their communities.


Communication and handoffs help connect those pieces. For example, a patient with diabetes received same-day support from an Ouma diabetes educator and MFM physician, and after Ouma helped address this immediate need, the patient was handed off to a local MFM specialist for ongoing care. In another case, Ouma coordinated behavioral health treatment with a patient’s OB-GYN and case management team while helping connect the patient with longer-term psychiatric care locally.


That flexibility matters in rural communities, where available resources can vary widely. When strong local services are available, virtual care can supplement them. When access is limited, virtual services can provide more comprehensive support while helping connect members with in-person care when needed.


## Measuring the Impact of Better Maternal Care Access


For individuals and families, better access ultimately needs to translate into better care and healthier outcomes. Measures that can help show whether programs are reaching that goal include:


- Timely prenatal and postpartum visits


- How quickly members can reach specialists


- Maternal and infant outcomes


- Behavioral health


- Member experience


- Equity


Ouma’s performance measures similarly focus on areas including prenatal and postpartum care, maternal and neonatal outcomes and access to behavioral healthcare.


Ouma’s broader tele-MFM results offer an example of what expanded virtual access can make possible. Ninety-four percent of patients receiving tele-MFM services are able to stay local rather than travel elsewhere for that expertise.


The goal is to make it easier for people in rural communities to get the care they need, when they need it. Connecting Centene’s care coordination with virtual maternity expertise and care available locally can help more people access support throughout pregnancy and postpartum, closer to home.


**Baseline established in 2025 via Centene’s MCH Ecology Dashboard.*
